arXiv:2610.06764v1 [quant-ph] 05 Oct 2026

Hypercontractivity and entropy decay for infinite-dimensional quantum Gibbs samplers

Simon Becker Address: Bocconi University, Milan, Italy Email address: simon.becker@unibocconi.it , Cambyse Rouzé Address: Inria, Télécom Paris–LTCI, Institut Polytechnique de Paris, 91120 Palaiseau, France Email address: cambyse.rouze@inria.fr and Robert Salzmann Address: Department of Physics, RWTH Aachen, Otto-Blumenthal-Strasse 20, 52074 Aachen, Germany Email address: robert.salzmann@rwth-aachen.de
Abstract.

We derive rates of exponential relative-entropy decay for a broad class of infinite-dimensional quantum Gibbs samplers. A key technical ingredient is a perturbative stability theory for hypercontractive estimates and logarithmic Sobolev inequalities. For suitably chosen dissipative couplings, we obtain exponential entropy decay for full multimode Bose–Hubbard samplers with arbitrary hopping and repulsive density interactions. For harmonically confined quantum Coulomb gases and molecular systems, we prove exponential entropy decay for every fixed finite-rank low-energy truncation of the interaction. Finally, we exhibit a periodic charging model with a positive spectral gap but no finite-time L2L^{2}-to-LpL^{p} bound for any p>2p>2.

Key words and phrases:
Quantum Markov semigroup, hypercontractivity, modified logarithmic Sobolev inequality, relative entropy, Gibbs sampler

1. Introduction and main results

Thermal-state preparation is a basic task in quantum statistical mechanics and quantum computation. A Gibbs sampler drives an initial state towards thermal equilibrium through a dissipative evolution. A spectral gap gives exponential decay of deviations from equilibrium in a weighted L2L^{2} norm. In infinite dimension, this estimate requires initial data in the weighted L2L^{2} space. Relative entropy measures distinguishability from equilibrium and, for a Gibbs state, equals the excess free energy divided by the temperature whenever these quantities are finite. Exponential relative-entropy estimates can also apply to initial states outside the weighted L2L^{2} space and control convergence in trace distance.

Boundedness of the semigroup from L2L^{2} to LpL^{p}, p>2p>2, connects L2L^{2} relaxation with relative-entropy decay. A finite L2L^{2}-to-LpL^{p} bound is referred to as hyperboundedness, while a bound with operator norm at most one is the contractive form of hypercontractivity. Both express an improvement in integrability after a finite time. This smoothing property is not implied by a spectral gap alone. In classical probability, the connection between hypercontractivity, logarithmic Sobolev inequalities, and convergence to equilibrium has been studied extensively since Gross’s foundational work; see [1]. These inequalities give estimates for diffusion and Markov-chain mixing. For reversible quantum dynamics, we show that one bounded L2L^{2}-to-LqL^{q} map gives an explicit exponential relative-entropy bound. In the atomic setting considered here, this endpoint already implies compact resolvent and, under primitivity, a positive spectral gap. Its value enters the rate when the endpoint norm exceeds one.

Efficient finite-dimensional quantum Gibbs samplers satisfying exact KMS detailed balance were developed in [2, 3], and the infinite-dimensional construction of [4] extends this framework to systems governed by unbounded Hamiltonians and jump operators. We study when these samplers improve integrability and how this gives entropy decay. We prove sufficient conditions and examples of failure, showing what must be added to a spectral-gap estimate. The behavior depends on the choice of jumps, even when the Hamiltonian is fixed.

1.1. Main results

We first state two criteria that turn a bounded L2L^{2}-to-LqL^{q} map into exponential relative-entropy decay. A state is a positive trace-class operator of trace one; it is faithful if its kernel is zero. Let Φt\Phi_{t}, t≥0t\geq 0, be a strongly continuous semigroup of completely positive, trace-preserving linear maps on trace-class operators, and let σ\sigma be a faithful invariant state. Write TtT_{t} for the dual evolution of observables. For 1≤p<∞1\leq p<\infty, the equilibrium-weighted space Lp​(σ)L^{p}(\sigma) is the completion of bounded observables in the norm

‖X‖p,σ=‖σ1/(2​p)​X​σ1/(2​p)‖p,\|X\|_{p,\sigma}=\|\sigma^{1/(2p)}X\sigma^{1/(2p)}\|_{p},

where ∥⋅∥p\|\cdot\|_{p} is the Schatten pp-norm. The space L∞​(σ)L^{\infty}(\sigma) consists of bounded observables with the operator norm. We assume that TtT_{t} extends consistently to positive contractions on these spaces, is self-adjoint on L2​(σ)L^{2}(\sigma), and has only scalar observables in its L2L^{2} fixed space. These are the reversibility and primitivity assumptions used below; reversibility is in the Kubo–Martin–Schwinger (KMS) sense.

With Tr\operatorname{Tr} denoting the operator trace, the spectral gap λ\lambda is the optimal exponential contraction rate on observables X∈L2​(σ)X\in L^{2}(\sigma) of equilibrium mean zero:

‖Tt​X‖2,σ≤e−λ​t​‖X‖2,σ,Tr⁡(σ​X)=0.\|T_{t}X\|_{2,\sigma}\leq e^{-\lambda t}\|X\|_{2,\sigma},\qquad\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma X)=0.

For X∈L2​(σ)X\in L^{2}(\sigma), the mean Tr⁡(σ​X)\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma X) denotes its continuous extension from bounded observables. The gap may vanish in infinite dimension. For a state ρ\rho, its relative entropy is

D(ρ∥σ)=Tr(ρ(logρ−logσ))∈[0,∞],D(\rho\|\sigma)=\operatorname{Tr}\bigl(\rho(\log\rho-\log\sigma)\bigr)\in[0,\infty],

interpreted in the extended sense when the separate traces are not finite. The spaces and operator domains are specified in Section 2.

Theorem 1.1 uses the Stroock–Varopoulos comparison: entropy production is at least four times the Dirichlet energy of the square root of the state. The domain requirement is included in (2.6) below.

Theorem 1.1.

In the reversible setting above, assume the Stroock–Varopoulos comparison (2.6). Suppose that, for some s>0s>0 and C≥1C\geq 1,

(1.1) ∥Ts:L2(σ)→L4(σ)∥≤C.\|T_{s}:L^{2}(\sigma)\to L^{4}(\sigma)\|\leq C.

If C>1C>1, let λ>0\lambda>0 denote the spectral gap, which is positive by the endpoint bound and primitivity. Then every state ρ\rho satisfies, for t≥0t\geq 0,

D(Φt(ρ)∥σ)≤e−αHC​tD(ρ∥σ),αHC=(s+log⁡C+12λ)−1.D(\Phi_{t}(\rho)\|\sigma)\leq e^{-\alpha_{\rm HC}t}D(\rho\|\sigma),\qquad\alpha_{\rm HC}=\left(s+\frac{\log C+\frac{1}{2}}{\lambda}\right)^{-1}.

If C=1C=1, the same conclusion holds with αHC=s−1\alpha_{\rm HC}=s^{-1} without a gap assumption.

The comparison can fail for the samplers considered here. The following result extends the finite-dimensional endpoint criterion of [5, Theorem 3.3] to the present setting, with the same entropy-decay rate after normalization.

In the same reversible setting, let q0>2q_{0}>2 and suppose that, for some s>0s>0 and C≥1C\geq 1,

∥Ts:L2(σ)→Lq0(σ)∥≤C.\|T_{s}:L^{2}(\sigma)\to L^{q_{0}}(\sigma)\|\leq C.

If C>1C>1, let λ>0\lambda>0 denote the spectral gap, which is positive by the endpoint bound and primitivity. Then every state ρ\rho satisfies, for t≥0t\geq 0,

(1.2) D(Φt(ρ)∥σ)≤e−αKMS​tD(ρ∥σ),αKMS=1−2/q0s+λ−1​(log⁡C+1−2/q0).D(\Phi_{t}(\rho)\|\sigma)\leq e^{-\alpha_{\rm KMS}t}D(\rho\|\sigma),\qquad\alpha_{\rm KMS}=\frac{1-2/q_{0}}{s+\lambda^{-1}(\log C+1-2/q_{0})}.

If C=1C=1, one may take αKMS=(1−2/q0)/s\alpha_{\rm KMS}=(1-2/q_{0})/s without a gap.

In Section 3, we prove two stability results. First, adding a bounded operator to the generator preserves the LpL^{p} bounds along a hypercontractive curve, provided its norm is uniformly bounded on those spaces. We give the resulting norm estimate. Second, a change of the Gibbs weight on a finite-dimensional energy subspace, apart from normalization, preserves a tight 22-logarithmic Sobolev inequality when the Dirichlet forms are comparable and the new generator has a positive gap.

The main applications are Bose–Hubbard and trapped Coulomb samplers. In both cases we prove the smoothing estimate and the positive gap needed by Theorem 1.2.

Bose–Hubbard models.

On a fixed lattice of kk modes, Theorem 4.3 treats

H=∑j=1k[Uj2​Nj​(Nj−I)−μj​Nj]+∑i<jVi​j​Ni​Nj−∑i<j(Ji​j​ai†​aj+Ji​j¯​aj†​ai),H=\sum_{j=1}^{k}\left[\frac{U_{j}}{2}N_{j}(N_{j}-I)-\mu_{j}N_{j}\right]+\sum_{i<j}V_{ij}N_{i}N_{j}-\sum_{i<j}\left(J_{ij}a_{i}^{\dagger}a_{j}+\overline{J_{ij}}a_{j}^{\dagger}a_{i}\right),

D(Φt(ρ)∥σβ)≤e−α​tD(ρ∥σβ),α>0.D(\Phi_{t}(\rho)\|\sigma_{\beta})\leq e^{-\alpha t}D(\rho\|\sigma_{\beta}),\qquad\alpha>0.

The theorem allows arbitrary hopping amplitudes and uses the full bosonic space, without an occupation cutoff. The cubic jumps provide losses of order n3n^{3} on the sector with nn particles; these dominate the quadratic energy and the errors caused by hopping. The same theorem gives a bounded endpoint after a positive waiting time with the smaller jump family aj,aj†,aj2,(aj†)2a_{j},a_{j}^{\dagger},a_{j}^{2},(a_{j}^{\dagger})^{2}. The rate may depend on the lattice size and all model parameters.

Trapped Coulomb systems.

For nn particles in d=2d=2 or 33 dimensions, Corollary 4.5 considers the Hamiltonian

Hn,M=−Δ+|x|2+ΠM​(∑i<jαn,i,j​wd​(xi−xj))​ΠM,w2​(y)=−log⁡|y|,w3​(y)=|y|−1,H_{n,M}=-\Delta+|x|^{2}+\Pi_{M}\left(\sum_{i<j}\alpha_{n,i,j}w_{d}(x_{i}-x_{j})\right)\Pi_{M},\qquad w_{2}(y)=-\log|y|,\quad w_{3}(y)=|y|^{-1},

where ΠM=PM⊗n\Pi_{M}=P_{M}^{\otimes n} and PMP_{M} projects onto the first MM one-particle Hermite functions, and the couplings αn,i,j\alpha_{n,i,j} are real. Only the interaction is truncated; the Hamiltonian acts on L2​((ℝd)n)L^{2}((\mathbb{R}^{d})^{n}). With coordinate creation and annihilation jumps and the Gaussian filter f^η​(ν)=e−η​ν2−β​ν/4\widehat{f}_{\eta}(\nu)=e^{-\eta\nu^{2}-\beta\nu/4}, η>0\eta>0, the sampler has a unique invariant Gibbs state and a positive gap. For each fixed n,Mn,M, we prove a contractive L2L^{2}-to-L4L^{4} bound after a finite time and exponential relative-entropy decay. The proof controls the terms containing one ladder operator and one finite-energy coefficient by a weighted oscillator estimate. The constants can depend on nn and MM.

The other examples explain when such smoothing estimates can fail. For one-mode polynomial number Hamiltonians, Theorem 4.2 compares the degree of the Hamiltonian with the largest jump order. Bounded L2L^{2}-to-LpL^{p} maps then occur at every positive time, after a positive waiting time, or never; the stated classification excludes the boundary time in the critical case. A periodic charging model has a positive gap but no such bound at any finite time.

1.2. Relation to earlier work

Our results build on finite-dimensional entropy criteria and on the infinite-dimensional Gibbs samplers constructed in earlier work. The finite-dimensional version of Theorem 1.2 is due to Gao and Wang [5, Theorem 3.3]. Their entropy-decay rate agrees with ours after converting their normalization D(Φt(ρ)∥σ)≤e−2​α1​tD(ρ∥σ)D(\Phi_{t}(\rho)\|\sigma)\leq e^{-2\alpha_{1}t}D(\rho\|\sigma). They combine weighted interpolation, contraction of centred observables, and a norm-to-entropy estimate. We extend their criterion to infinite dimension. We approximate arbitrary states while preserving the limit of the relative entropy, and prove the required L2L^{2}-to-LqL^{q} bounds for our unbounded models. Related finite-dimensional results for primitive KMS-symmetric semigroups appear in [6, 7].

Noncommutative hypercontractivity and its connection with logarithmic Sobolev inequalities go back to the weighted LpL^{p} theory of [8]; see also [9, 10]. Complete modified logarithmic Sobolev inequalities and their tensor-stable finite-dimensional forms were developed in [11], while perturbative change-of-measure principles appear in [12]. The equivalence between modified logarithmic Sobolev inequalities and exponential relative-entropy decay in the von Neumann algebra setting is treated in [13]. Here one L2L^{2}-to-LqL^{q} bound in infinite dimension gives an explicit entropy-decay rate, involving the automatically positive spectral gap when the bound has norm greater than one. One argument uses the Stroock–Varopoulos comparison; the other uses only the KMS reversibility assumptions above. The counterexample in Proposition 2.10 shows why the KMS argument is needed for general cross-frequency generators.

Our earlier work [4] provides the infinite-dimensional Gibbs-sampler construction used here. In [14], we established spectral-gap results for mean-field and full multimode Bose–Hubbard samplers and used them to obtain thermal-state preparation guarantees. Here we prove the additional smoothing estimates needed for exponential decay from every initial state of finite relative entropy. This requires control of the jump operators as well as the Hamiltonian. For example, for H=N2H=N^{2} and the filter used in Section 4.1, Theorem 4.2 shows that linear jumps alone have no bounded L2L^{2}-to-L4L^{4} endpoint, whereas adding cubic jumps gives such a bound at every positive time and yields the entropy estimate in Theorem 4.3. Quadratic jumps already give an endpoint after a positive waiting time, including with hopping; cubic jumps give the every-positive-time conclusion. The theorem does not give the same entropy estimate for the linear-jump samplers of [14].

The Coulomb result complements the fixed-cutoff spectral-gap analysis of [15]. We prove a weighted oscillator estimate for the perturbed semigroup, controlling the mixed terms that contain one unbounded ladder operator. This gives an L2L^{2}-to-L4L^{4} bound directly. The form comparison in Section 3 also preserves a tight 22-logarithmic Sobolev inequality, but obtaining hypercontractivity from that inequality would require an additional regularity assumption.

Section 2 sets up the spaces and proves the entropy-decay criteria. Section 3 proves the stability results, and Section 4 treats the bosonic examples and obstructions.

1.3. AI statement

We used OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-6 Astra to help identify assumptions under which generators associated with bosonic Hamiltonians, particularly the Bose–Hubbard Hamiltonian, are hypercontractive. We also used these tools to assist with manuscript preparation. We reviewed and verified the AI-assisted material and take full responsibility for the content of this work.

2. Framework and entropy decay

We define the weighted spaces and prove the two entropy-decay criteria from the introduction. The first proof uses a logarithmic Sobolev inequality and the Stroock–Varopoulos comparison; the second obtains entropy contraction directly from KMS symmetry and hypercontractivity. We then show why the comparison can fail when different frequencies are coupled, and give approximation conditions that extend it to infinite-dimensional Davies generators.

We define the operator spaces, Gibbs samplers, and reversibility assumptions used throughout the paper.

Compactness from one endpoint.

For 2<q<∞2<q<\infty, the inclusion Lq​(σ)↪L2​(σ)L^{q}(\sigma)\hookrightarrow L^{2}(\sigma) is compact. In symmetric Schatten coordinates it is Jq​(Y)=σa​Y​σaJ_{q}(Y)=\sigma^{a}Y\sigma^{a}, where a=1/4−1/(2​q)>0a=1/4-1/(2q)>0. For finite-rank spectral projections Pn↑IP_{n}\uparrow I of σ\sigma, Schatten Hölder with r=1/ar=1/a and 2/r+1/q=1/22/r+1/q=1/2 gives

‖Jq−Pn​Jq​(⋅)​Pn‖𝒯q→𝒯2≤2​(Tr⁡((I−Pn)​σ))a⟶0.\|J_{q}-P_{n}J_{q}(\,\cdot\,)P_{n}\|_{\mathscr{T}_{q}\to\mathscr{T}_{2}}\leq 2\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}((I-P_{n})\sigma)\bigr)^{a}\longrightarrow 0.

The approximating maps have finite rank. Thus a bounded Ts:L2​(σ)→Lq​(σ)T_{s}:L^{2}(\sigma)\to L^{q}(\sigma) makes e−s​Le^{-sL} compact. The spectral theorem then gives compact resolvent for LL; if ker⁡L=ℂ​σ\ker L=\mathbb{C}\sqrt{\sigma}, zero is simple and isolated, so gap⁡(L)>0\operatorname{gap}(L)>0. This argument uses the atomic algebra B⁡(ℋ)B(\mathcal{H}) and trace-class σ\sigma; it does not assert compactness for diffuse algebras or a uniform numerical lower bound on the gap.

Let ℒ(p)\mathscr{L}^{(p)} denote the generator of Tt(p)T_{t}^{(p)} on Lp​(σ)L^{p}(\sigma). The minus sign in (2.4) gives

L=−ι2,σ​ℒ(2)​ι2,σ−1.L=-\iota_{2,\sigma}\mathscr{L}^{(2)}\iota_{2,\sigma}^{-1}.

The Bohr frequencies are the energy differences in Ω(H)={E′−E:E,E′∈Sp(H)}\Omega(H)=\{E^{\prime}-E:E,E^{\prime}\in\operatorname{Sp}(H)\}. Let σE∈(0,∞]\sigma_{E}\in(0,\infty] be an energy-resolution width: the sampler couples energy differences ν\nu and μ\mu with Gaussian factor exp[−(ν−μ)2/(8σE2)]\exp[-(\nu-\mu)^{2}/(8\sigma_{E}^{2})], interpreted as one when σE=∞\sigma_{E}=\infty. With the filter f^\widehat{f} and Hamiltonian HH fixed, write ℒσE\mathcal{L}_{\sigma_{E}} for the state-side generator and LσE≥0L_{\sigma_{E}}\geq 0 for its standard-form operator. The explicit finite-dimensional formula is (2.20). At the Davies endpoint σE=0\sigma_{E}=0, only equal frequencies remain; its form is denoted by ℰ0\mathcal{E}_{0} and is generated by L0L_{0}.

We call the family hyperbounded if for every 1<p<q<∞1<p<q<\infty there are τp,q≥0\tau_{p,q}\geq 0 and Cp,q≥1C_{p,q}\geq 1 such that

(2.5) ∥Tt(p):Lp(σ)→Lq(σ)∥≤Cp,q,t>τp,q.\|T_{t}^{(p)}:L^{p}(\sigma)\to L^{q}(\sigma)\|\leq C_{p,q},\qquad t>\tau_{p,q}.

We call an LpL^{p}-to-LqL^{q} bound contractive if its norm is at most one. An endpoint bound means an LpL^{p}-to-LqL^{q} bound at one fixed time.

2.2. Relative entropy and entropy production

We introduce entropy production and formulate the entropy-decay criteria for Gibbs samplers with filtered jumps.

We use the Umegaki relative entropy introduced in Section 1.1, written D(ρ∥ω)D(\rho\|\omega) for a faithful reference state ω\omega. Logarithms are defined by functional calculus, with 0​log⁡0=00\log 0=0; in infinite dimension the trace expression is understood in the extended relative-entropy sense, rather than as a difference of two possibly infinite traces [21, Section 2 and Remark 4.6]. We use trace-norm lower semicontinuity and data processing in this extended sense; see [21, Theorem 4.1(i),(iv)]. Let

B(ω)=⋃Γ≥1{ρ∈𝒯1(ℋ):ρ≥0,Trρ=1,Γ−1ω≤ρ≤Γω}.B(\omega)=\bigcup_{\Gamma\geq 1}\{\rho\in\mathscr{T}_{1}(\mathcal{H}):\rho\geq 0,\ \operatorname{Tr}\rho=1,\ \Gamma^{-1}\omega\leq\rho\leq\Gamma\omega\}.

Here the inequalities are in the operator order and Γ\Gamma is a scalar comparison constant. The notation B⁡(ω)B(\omega) denotes this set of states, whereas B⁡(ℋ)B(\mathcal{H}) denotes the algebra of bounded operators. For ρ∈D⁡(ℒ)∩B⁡(ω)\rho\in D(\mathcal{L})\cap B(\omega) and an invariant state ω\omega, the entropy production is

EPℒ⁡(ρ)=−Tr⁡(ℒ⁡(ρ)​(log⁡ρ−log⁡ω)).\operatorname{EP}_{\mathcal{L}}(\rho)=-\operatorname{Tr}\bigl(\mathcal{L}(\rho)(\log\rho-\log\omega)\bigr).

The logarithmic difference has a bounded extension on B⁡(ω)B(\omega), so this trace is defined. A modified logarithmic Sobolev inequality (MLSI) with rate α>0\alpha>0 is αD(ρ∥ω)≤EPℒ(ρ)\alpha D(\rho\|\omega)\leq\operatorname{EP}_{\mathcal{L}}(\rho) on this domain. The precise Stroock–Varopoulos (SV) assumption in Theorem 1.1 is that, for every ρ∈D⁡(ℒ)∩B⁡(σ)\rho\in D(\mathcal{L})\cap B(\sigma),

(2.6) ρ∈D⁡(ℰ),4​ℰ​(ρ)≤EPℒ⁡(ρ).\sqrt{\rho}\in D(\mathcal{E}),\qquad 4\mathcal{E}(\sqrt{\rho})\leq\operatorname{EP}_{\mathcal{L}}(\rho).

KMS symmetry alone does not imply this comparison; see Proposition 2.10. Under the assumptions of Theorem 1.1, the proof also gives the equivalent MLSI,

αHCD(ρ∥σ)≤EPℒ(ρ),ρ∈D(ℒ)∩B(σ),\alpha_{\rm HC}D(\rho\|\sigma)\leq\operatorname{EP}_{\mathcal{L}}(\rho),\qquad\rho\in D(\mathcal{L})\cap B(\sigma),

with the same rate αHC\alpha_{\rm HC} as in Theorem 1.1.

Theorem 1.2 applies to the filtered samplers as follows.

Corollary 2.1.

Let σE∈(0,∞]\sigma_{E}\in(0,\infty] and let Φt=et​ℒσE\Phi_{t}=e^{t\mathcal{L}_{\sigma_{E}}} be any of the conservative KMS-symmetric semigroups constructed in [4], with invariant Gibbs state σβ\sigma_{\beta}. Assume the irreducibility hypotheses giving ker⁡LσE=ℂ​σβ\ker L_{\sigma_{E}}=\mathbb{C}\sqrt{\sigma_{\beta}}, and put L=LσE≥0L=L_{\sigma_{E}}\geq 0 in the sign convention of (2.4). If

∥Ts(2):L2(σβ)→L4(σβ)∥≤C>1,\|T_{s}^{(2)}:L^{2}(\sigma_{\beta})\to L^{4}(\sigma_{\beta})\|\leq C>1,

then λ=gap⁡(L)>0\lambda=\operatorname{gap}(L)>0 and (1.2) holds with

(2.7) αKMS=(2​s+2​log⁡C+1λ)−1.\alpha_{\rm KMS}=\left(2s+\frac{2\log C+1}{\lambda}\right)^{-1}.

For C=1C=1, the rate (2​s)−1(2s)^{-1} holds without a gap. This includes the original generator at σE=∞\sigma_{E}=\infty and every Gaussian width 0<σE<∞0<\sigma_{E}<\infty; it does not use the Davies limit σE=0\sigma_{E}=0.

For the same L2L^{2}-to-L4L^{4} bound at time ss, with constant C>1C>1 and spectral gap λ>0\lambda>0, the two entropy-decay rates are

αHC=(s+log⁡C+1/2λ)−1,αKMS=12​αHC.\alpha_{\rm HC}=\left(s+\frac{\log C+1/2}{\lambda}\right)^{-1},\qquad\alpha_{\rm KMS}=\frac{1}{2}\alpha_{\rm HC}.

Theorem 1.1 gives the first rate when the Stroock–Varopoulos comparison holds. Theorem 1.2 gives the second rate without that comparison. The KMS argument therefore gives half the rate obtained with SV. Proposition 2.10 shows why the comparison cannot be assumed for cross-frequency generators; it does not show that this factor of two is optimal.

Hyperboundedness gives an L2L^{2}-to-L4L^{4} bound after the waiting time τ2,4\tau_{2,4} in (2.5). Under primitivity, compactness gives a positive gap, and Theorem 1.2 therefore gives exponential relative-entropy decay. If the Stroock–Varopoulos comparison also holds, Theorem 1.1 gives the faster rate above. A unique invariant state does not by itself ensure a positive gap in infinite dimension. When the L2L^{2}-to-L4L^{4} bound has norm at most one, Theorem 1.2 gives the rate (2​s)−1(2s)^{-1} without a gap. If the Stroock–Varopoulos comparison holds as well, Theorem 1.1 improves this rate to s−1s^{-1}.

The following table compares the two entropy-decay criteria. In the first two rows the endpoint bound has constant C>1C>1, and its automatically positive spectral gap enters the rate; in the last two rows the endpoint is contractive (C=1C=1), so the rate needs no gap value.

Norm bound Other assumptions Entropy-decay rate
L2→L4L^{2}\to L^{4} at (s,C)(s,C) SV (s+log⁡C+1/2λ)−1\displaystyle\left(s+\frac{\log C+1/2}{\lambda}\right)^{-1}
L2→Lq0L^{2}\to L^{q_{0}} at (s,C)(s,C) KMS symmetry 1−2/q0s+λ−1​(log⁡C+1−2/q0)\displaystyle\frac{1-2/q_{0}}{s+\lambda^{-1}(\log C+1-2/q_{0})}
contractive L2→L4L^{2}\to L^{4} SV s−1s^{-1}
contractive L2→Lq0L^{2}\to L^{q_{0}} KMS symmetry (1−2/q0)​s−1(1-2/q_{0})s^{-1}

To prove Theorem 1.1, we first derive a logarithmic Sobolev inequality. We interpolate the L2L^{2}-to-L4L^{4} bound to small times and differentiate at time zero. This gives a 22-logarithmic Sobolev inequality with an additional squared-norm term, called the defect. The Rothaus estimate transfers the defect to the component orthogonal to the invariant vector, and the Poincaré inequality bounds this component by the Dirichlet energy. Combining the tight inequality with the Stroock–Varopoulos comparison gives the modified logarithmic Sobolev inequality. Exponential relative-entropy decay then follows. When C=1C=1, differentiation already gives a tight inequality, so the gap is unnecessary.

The proof of Theorem 1.2 derives entropy contraction directly from the weighted LpL^{p} estimates. For C>1C>1, interpolation, noncommutative LqL^{q} smoothness, and decay of centred observables under the spectral gap yield contractive L2L^{2}-to-LqL^{q} bounds after an explicit additional time. KMS symmetry then allows interpolation with the L1L^{1} contraction to give a strong data-processing inequality for relative entropy. We divide the time interval into equal pieces and iterate the short-time estimate. Letting the number of pieces tend to infinity gives exponential decay. Optimizing the interpolation parameter gives the rate in Theorem 1.2. For C=1C=1, the argument starts from the given contractive endpoint and again requires no gap.

The remainder of Section 2 proves these criteria and identifies the cross-frequency obstruction to the Stroock–Varopoulos comparison. Its infinite-dimensional Davies criterion is conditional on the stated exhaustion hypotheses, which must be verified for any proposed application. Section 3 proves stability of the norm bounds under bounded perturbations, and of 22-logarithmic Sobolev inequalities under changes of the Gibbs weight on a finite energy subspace. Section 4 treats polynomial jumps, Bose–Hubbard samplers with hopping, and finite-rank Coulomb perturbations of tensor quantum Ornstein–Uhlenbeck (qOU) semigroups. It also gives the periodic charging example.

2.3. Modified logarithmic Sobolev inequality

We relate the modified logarithmic Sobolev inequality to entropy decay and express relative entropy in the Hilbert–Schmidt representation.

If Γ−1​ω≤ρ≤Γ​ω\Gamma^{-1}\omega\leq\rho\leq\Gamma\omega, operator monotonicity of the logarithm shows that the quadratic-form difference log⁡ρ−log⁡ω\log\rho-\log\omega extends to a bounded self-adjoint operator, with

‖log⁡ρ−log⁡ω‖∞≤log⁡Γ;\|\log\rho-\log\omega\|_{\infty}\leq\log\Gamma;

see [19]. Thus its pairing with ℒ​(ρ)∈𝒯1​(ℋ)\mathcal{L}(\rho)\in\mathscr{T}_{1}(\mathcal{H}) is defined for ρ∈D⁡(ℒ)∩B⁡(ω)\rho\in D(\mathcal{L})\cap B(\omega).

Lemma 2.2.

Let ω\omega be a faithful invariant state of Φt=et​ℒ\Phi_{t}=e^{t\mathcal{L}} and let α>0\alpha>0. The estimate D(Φt(ρ)∥ω)≤e−α​tD(ρ∥ω)D(\Phi_{t}(\rho)\|\omega)\leq e^{-\alpha t}D(\rho\|\omega) for all states and all t≥0t\geq 0 is equivalent to

αD(ρ∥ω)≤EPℒ(ρ),ρ∈D(ℒ)∩B(ω).\alpha D(\rho\|\omega)\leq\operatorname{EP}_{\mathcal{L}}(\rho),\qquad\rho\in D(\mathcal{L})\cap B(\omega).

This is the equivalence between MLSI and entropy decay in infinite dimension; see [13, Lemma A.1 and Theorem 2.7].

The hypercontractive estimates use the spaces Lp​(σ)L^{p}(\sigma), whereas the Dirichlet form acts on the fixed Hilbert space 𝒯2​(ℋ)\mathscr{T}_{2}(\mathcal{H}). We identify an observable XX with

Y=ι2,σ​(X)=σ1/4​X​σ1/4.Y=\iota_{2,\sigma}(X)=\sigma^{1/4}X\sigma^{1/4}.

This identification is isometric: ‖Y‖2=‖X‖2,σ\|Y\|_{2}=\|X\|_{2,\sigma}. The norm of the same observable in Lp​(σ)L^{p}(\sigma) is obtained by changing the weights from σ1/4\sigma^{1/4} to σ1/(2​p)\sigma^{1/(2p)}. In terms of YY, this gives

(2.8) ‖Y‖p←2,σ:=‖σ1/(2​p)−1/4​Y​σ1/(2​p)−1/4‖p=‖X‖p,σ,1≤p<∞,\|Y\|_{p\leftarrow 2,\sigma}:=\|\sigma^{1/(2p)-1/4}Y\sigma^{1/(2p)-1/4}\|_{p}=\|X\|_{p,\sigma},\qquad 1\leq p<\infty,

whenever these norms are finite. The subscript p←2p\leftarrow 2 denotes the weighted LpL^{p} norm in the Hilbert–Schmidt coordinates fixed at p=2p=2. At p=2p=2, it is the ordinary Hilbert–Schmidt norm.

For p>2p>2, the exponent of σ\sigma in (2.8) is negative. Since the eigenvalues of σ\sigma can approach zero, this expression need not be finite for every Hilbert–Schmidt operator. We define it by finite spectral cutoffs. Choose increasing finite-rank spectral projections PnP_{n} of σ\sigma with Pn→IP_{n}\to I strongly, and set

‖Y‖p←2,σ=limn→∞‖σ1/(2​p)−1/4​Pn​Y​Pn​σ1/(2​p)−1/4‖p∈[0,∞].\|Y\|_{p\leftarrow 2,\sigma}=\lim_{n\to\infty}\|\sigma^{1/(2p)-1/4}P_{n}YP_{n}\sigma^{1/(2p)-1/4}\|_{p}\in[0,\infty].

All powers in each term act on the finite-dimensional range of PnP_{n}. The norms increase with nn, and their limit is independent of the chosen exhaustion. The domain consists of those YY for which this limit is finite; on that domain the reweighted operator belongs to 𝒯p​(ℋ)\mathscr{T}_{p}(\mathcal{H}). The proof of Theorem 2.3 constructs the form core used to differentiate the semigroup.

For Y∈𝒯2​(ℋ)∖{0}Y\in\mathscr{T}_{2}(\mathcal{H})\setminus\{0\}, define

Ent2,σ(Y):=‖Y‖222[\displaystyle\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma}(Y):=\frac{\|Y\|_{2}^{2}}{2}\bigg[ D(Y†​Y‖Y‖22∥σ)+D(Y​Y†‖Y‖22∥σ)],\displaystyle D\left(\frac{Y^{\dagger}Y}{\|Y\|_{2}^{2}}\middle\|\sigma\right)+D\left(\frac{YY^{\dagger}}{\|Y\|_{2}^{2}}\middle\|\sigma\right)\bigg],

with Ent2,σ⁡(0)=0\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma}(0)=0 and infinite values allowed. Both normalized operators inside the relative entropies are states, and this functional is lower semicontinuous in the Hilbert–Schmidt norm. For YY supported on a finite spectral subspace of σ\sigma, differentiating (2.8) gives

Ent2,σ⁡(Y)=4​‖Y‖22​dd​p​log⁡‖Y‖p←2,σ|p=2,Y≠0.\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma}(Y)=4\|Y\|_{2}^{2}\left.\frac{\,\mathrm{d}}{\,\mathrm{d}p}\log\|Y\|_{p\leftarrow 2,\sigma}\right|_{p=2},\qquad Y\neq 0.

In particular, a state ρ\rho is represented in the positive cone of Hilbert–Schmidt space by its square root Y=ρY=\sqrt{\rho}. Then Y†​Y=Y​Y†=ρY^{\dagger}Y=YY^{\dagger}=\rho and ‖Y‖22=Tr⁡ρ=1\|Y\|_{2}^{2}=\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1, so

2.4. The Gross and Rothaus steps

We differentiate the hypercontractive bound and use the Rothaus and Poincaré inequalities to obtain a tight logarithmic Sobolev inequality.

For standard-form vectors use the complex Hilbert–Schmidt inner product ⟨X,Y⟩:=Tr⁡(X†​Y)\langle X,Y\rangle:=\operatorname{Tr}(X^{\dagger}Y). Thus ⟨σ,X⟩​σ\langle\sqrt{\sigma},X\rangle\sqrt{\sigma} is the orthogonal projection of XX onto the invariant line ℂ​σ\mathbb{C}\sqrt{\sigma}.

Theorem 2.3.

Under the semigroup assumptions of Theorem 1.1, the endpoint (1.1) implies, for every standard-form vector X∈D⁡(ℰ)⊂𝒯2​(ℋ)X\in D(\mathcal{E})\subset\mathscr{T}_{2}(\mathcal{H}),

(2.9) Ent2,σ⁡(X)≤4​s​ℰ​(X)+4​log⁡C​‖X‖22.\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma}(X)\leq 4s\mathcal{E}(X)+4\log C\|X\|_{2}^{2}.

≤limR→∞(4​s​ℰ​(XR)+4​log⁡C​‖XR‖22)=4​s​ℰ​(X)+4​log⁡C​‖X‖22.\displaystyle\leq\lim_{R\to\infty}\bigl(4s\mathcal{E}(X_{R})+4\log C\|X_{R}\|_{2}^{2}\bigr)=4s\mathcal{E}(X)+4\log C\|X\|_{2}^{2}.

Lemma 2.4 (Rothaus inequality on the entropy domain).

Let σ\sigma be a faithful density matrix on ℋ\mathcal{H}. For every Y∈𝒯2​(ℋ)Y\in\mathscr{T}_{2}(\mathcal{H}) and a∈ℂa\in\mathbb{C},

∂q‖Z‖q←2,σ2|q=2+=2​‖Z‖22​∂qlog⁡‖Z‖q←2,σ|q=2+=12​Ent2,σ⁡(Z).\left.\partial_{q}\|Z\|_{q\leftarrow 2,\sigma}^{2}\right|_{q=2+}=2\|Z\|_{2}^{2}\left.\partial_{q}\log\|Z\|_{q\leftarrow 2,\sigma}\right|_{q=2+}=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma}(Z).

2.5. Entropy decay from KMS symmetry

We prove Theorem 1.2 by turning the hypercontractive bound into entropy contraction through weighted interpolation and noncommutative LqL^{q} smoothness.

We use the standard centred smoothness estimate

(2.14) ‖a​I+Y‖q,σ2≤|a|2+(q−1)​‖Y‖q,σ2,2≤q<∞,⟨Y⟩σ=0.\|aI+Y\|_{q,\sigma}^{2}\leq|a|^{2}+(q-1)\|Y\|_{q,\sigma}^{2},\qquad 2\leq q<\infty,\quad\langle Y\rangle_{\sigma}=0.

It is the Ball–Carlen–Lieb inequality [24] applied at a​σ1/qa\sigma^{1/q} in direction ιq,σ​(Y)\iota_{q,\sigma}(Y); the first variation vanishes by centering. Schatten-norm density extends the matrix inequality to the present Hilbert space. This is also the estimate used in [5, Lemma 2.3]. The next lemma gives the extra time needed to make the norm at most one.

Lemma 2.5.

∥Tu:L2(σ)→Lq(σ)∥≤K,\|T_{u}:L^{2}(\sigma)\to L^{q}(\sigma)\|\leq K,

⟨Tt​Y⟩σ=0,Tt​I=I,‖X‖2,σ2=|a|2+‖Y‖2,σ2.\langle T_{t}Y\rangle_{\sigma}=0,\qquad T_{t}I=I,\qquad\|X\|_{2,\sigma}^{2}=|a|^{2}+\|Y\|_{2,\sigma}^{2}.

‖Tu​Tr​Y‖q,σ≤K​‖Tr​Y‖2,σ≤K​e−λ​r​‖Y‖2,σ.\|T_{u}T_{r}Y\|_{q,\sigma}\leq K\|T_{r}Y\|_{2,\sigma}\leq Ke^{-\lambda r}\|Y\|_{2,\sigma}.

‖Tu+r​X‖q,σ2\displaystyle\|T_{u+r}X\|_{q,\sigma}^{2} =‖a​I+Tu​Tr​Y‖q,σ2\displaystyle=\|aI+T_{u}T_{r}Y\|_{q,\sigma}^{2}
≤|a|2+(q−1)​‖Tu​Tr​Y‖q,σ2≤|a|2+(q−1)​K2​e−2​λ​r​‖Y‖2,σ2.\displaystyle\leq|a|^{2}+(q-1)\|T_{u}T_{r}Y\|_{q,\sigma}^{2}\leq|a|^{2}+(q-1)K^{2}e^{-2\lambda r}\|Y\|_{2,\sigma}^{2}.

The time in (2.15) solves (q−1)​K2​e−2​λ​r=1(q-1)K^{2}e^{-2\lambda r}=1. The last expression is therefore ‖X‖2,σ2\|X\|_{2,\sigma}^{2}. ∎

Lemma 2.6.

For every state ρ\rho there are ρk∈B⁡(σ)\rho_{k}\in B(\sigma) such that

(2.16) ∥ρk−ρ∥1⟶0,D(ρk∥σ)⟶D(ρ∥σ)\|\rho_{k}-\rho\|_{1}\longrightarrow 0,\qquad D(\rho_{k}\|\sigma)\longrightarrow D(\rho\|\sigma)

∥ρε−ρ∥1≤2ε,D(ρε∥σ)≤(1−ε)D(ρ∥σ).\|\rho_{\varepsilon}-\rho\|_{1}\leq 2\varepsilon,\qquad D(\rho_{\varepsilon}\|\sigma)\leq(1-\varepsilon)D(\rho\|\sigma).

𝖤n​(ρ)=En​ρ​En+Tr⁡(Qn​ρ)​Qn​σ​QnTr⁡(Qn​σ).\mathsf{E}_{n}(\rho)=E_{n}\rho E_{n}+\operatorname{Tr}(Q_{n}\rho)\frac{Q_{n}\sigma Q_{n}}{\operatorname{Tr}(Q_{n}\sigma)}.

Tr⁡𝖤n​(ρ)=Tr⁡(En​ρ)+Tr⁡(Qn​ρ)=1,𝖤n​(σ)=σ.\operatorname{Tr}\mathsf{E}_{n}(\rho)=\operatorname{Tr}(E_{n}\rho)+\operatorname{Tr}(Q_{n}\rho)=1,\qquad\mathsf{E}_{n}(\sigma)=\sigma.

‖𝖤n​(ρ)−ρ‖1≤‖En​ρ​En−ρ‖1+Tr⁡(Qn​ρ)⟶0.\|\mathsf{E}_{n}(\rho)-\rho\|_{1}\leq\|E_{n}\rho E_{n}-\rho\|_{1}+\operatorname{Tr}(Q_{n}\rho)\longrightarrow 0.

cn=max⁡{‖En​ρ​En‖∞mn,Tr⁡(Qn​ρ)Tr⁡(Qn​σ)}.c_{n}=\max\left\{\frac{\|E_{n}\rho E_{n}\|_{\infty}}{m_{n}},\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(Q_{n}\rho)}{\operatorname{Tr}(Q_{n}\sigma)}\right\}.

εn​σ≤ρn≤((1−εn)​cn+εn)​σ,‖ρn−ρ‖1≤‖𝖤n​(ρ)−ρ‖1+2​εn→0.\varepsilon_{n}\sigma\leq\rho_{n}\leq\bigl((1-\varepsilon_{n})c_{n}+\varepsilon_{n}\bigr)\sigma,\qquad\|\rho_{n}-\rho\|_{1}\leq\|\mathsf{E}_{n}(\rho)-\rho\|_{1}+2\varepsilon_{n}\to 0.

The norm-to-entropy implication below is [26, Proposition 5.4] in finite dimension. We give the proof for unbounded Gibbs weights and arbitrary normal states.

Lemma 2.7.

Let Φ\Phi be a normal channel with faithful invariant state σ\sigma, let T=Φ∗T=\Phi^{*}, and assume that TT is σ\sigma-KMS symmetric and extends consistently to positive contractions on Lr​(σ)L^{r}(\sigma) for 1≤r≤∞1\leq r\leq\infty. Suppose that, for some 1≤K<∞1\leq K<\infty,

For a general state with finite input entropy, choose ρk\rho_{k} from Lemma 2.6. Trace-norm contractivity gives ‖Φ⁡(ρk)−Φ⁡(ρ)‖1≤‖ρk−ρ‖1→0\|\Phi(\rho_{k})-\Phi(\rho)\|_{1}\leq\|\rho_{k}-\rho\|_{1}\to 0. Consequently

≤limk((p−1)​qp⁡(q−1)D(ρk∥σ)+qq−1logK)\displaystyle\leq\lim_{k}\left(\frac{(p-1)q}{p(q-1)}D(\rho_{k}\|\sigma)+\frac{q}{q-1}\log K\right)

For infinite input entropy the right-hand side is infinite, so the assertion holds in the extended sense. ∎

Proof of Corollary 2.1.

The construction is a conservative KMS-symmetric QMS of positive contractions on the weighted scale, with invariant state σβ\sigma_{\beta}. Here KnK_{n} is extended by zero on (Pn​ℋ)⟂(P_{n}\mathcal{H})^{\perp}. The exhaustion is SV-admissible on a class of states if these conditions hold for every state in that class.

Uniform boundedness and strong convergence of KnK_{n}, together with trace-norm generator convergence, imply

(2.28) EPℒn⁡(ρn)=−Tr⁡(ℒn​(ρn)​Kn)⟶−Tr⁡(ℒ0​(ρ)​Kρ)=EPℒ0⁡(ρ).\operatorname{EP}_{\mathcal{L}_{n}}(\rho_{n})=-\operatorname{Tr}(\mathcal{L}_{n}(\rho_{n})K_{n})\longrightarrow-\operatorname{Tr}(\mathcal{L}_{0}(\rho)K_{\rho})=\operatorname{EP}_{\mathcal{L}_{0}}(\rho).

+|Tr⁡(ℒ0​(ρ)​(Kn−Kρ))|⟶0.\displaystyle+|\operatorname{Tr}(\mathcal{L}_{0}(\rho)(K_{n}-K_{\rho}))|\longrightarrow 0.

The first term vanishes by (2.27). For the second, approximate ℒ0​(ρ)\mathcal{L}_{0}(\rho) in trace norm by a finite-rank operator. Strong convergence handles that finite-rank pairing, and the uniform bound on KnK_{n} controls the approximation error.

Theorem 2.12.

Suppose that an SV-admissible exhaustion exists on D⁡(ℒ0)∩B⁡(σβ)D(\mathcal{L}_{0})\cap B(\sigma_{\beta}). Then the Stroock–Varopoulos hypothesis (2.6) of Theorem 1.1 holds on this class. For a primitive finite-dimensional Davies generator, Proposition 2.8 proves the SV inequality. Hence Theorem 1.1 applies if the weighted extensions are positive contractions, satisfy (2.4), and obey (1.1). The same conclusion holds in infinite dimension under Definition 2.11.

4cLSD(ρ∥σ)≤4ℰ(ρ)≤EPℒ(ρ).\frac{4}{c_{\rm LS}}D(\rho\|\sigma)\leq 4\mathcal{E}(\sqrt{\rho})\leq\operatorname{EP}_{\mathcal{L}}(\rho).

αHC=4cLS={(s+log⁡C+1/2λ)−1,C>1,s−1,C=1.\alpha_{\rm HC}=\frac{4}{c_{\rm LS}}=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\left(s+\frac{\log C+1/2}{\lambda}\right)^{-1},&C>1,\\[4.0pt] s^{-1},&C=1.\end{cases}

3. Perturbative hypercontractivity

We prove two stability results. With the Gibbs weight fixed, a product formula controls changes of the generator that are bounded along a hypercontractive curve. When the weight changes on a finite energy subspace, entropy and form comparisons preserve a tight logarithmic Sobolev inequality, provided the new generator has a positive gap.

3.1. Interpolation and bounded perturbations

We transfer bounds along a hypercontractive curve under perturbations that are bounded on each weighted space along the curve.

We use weighted Stein interpolation [22, 17] in the form established in Step 2 of Theorem 2.3; a weighted three-lines theorem is [23, Theorem 2.10]. For a KMS-symmetric semigroup as in Section 2, an endpoint ∥Tτ:L2(σ)→Lq(σ)∥≤C\|T_{\tau}:L^{2}(\sigma)\to L^{q}(\sigma)\|\leq C with τ>0\tau>0 and 2<q<∞2<q<\infty gives

∥Tt:L2(σ)→Lq⁡(t)(σ)∥≤Ct/τ,1q⁡(t)=1−t/τ2+t/τq,0≤t≤τ.\|T_{t}:L^{2}(\sigma)\to L^{q(t)}(\sigma)\|\leq C^{t/\tau},\qquad\frac{1}{q(t)}=\frac{1-t/\tau}{2}+\frac{t/\tau}{q},\quad 0\leq t\leq\tau.

The next theorem assumes a bound between every two points on the exponent curve. It is related to the Holley–Stroock principles of [1, 12]. For the bounded perturbation theorem and the Trotter product formula on a fixed Banach space, see [27, Theorem III.1.3 and Corollary III.5.8].

Theorem 3.1.

Let σ\sigma be a faithful density matrix, fix t∗>0t_{*}>0 and 2≤p∗<∞2\leq p_{*}<\infty, and let Tt(r)T_{t}^{(r)} and St(r)S_{t}^{(r)} be strongly continuous, consistent semigroups on Lr​(σ)L^{r}(\sigma) for 2≤r≤p∗2\leq r\leq p_{*}. Fix ω∈ℝ\omega\in\mathbb{R} and a continuous nondecreasing exponent curve p:[0,t∗]→[2,p∗]p:[0,t_{*}]\to[2,p_{*}] with p⁡(0)=2p(0)=2. Suppose that

∥Tt−s:Lp⁡(s)(σ)→Lp⁡(t)(σ)∥≤eω⁡(t−s),0≤s≤t≤t∗.\|T_{t-s}:L^{p(s)}(\sigma)\to L^{p(t)}(\sigma)\|\leq e^{\omega(t-s)},\qquad 0\leq s\leq t\leq t_{*}.

Let 𝒞\mathscr{C} be a common dense subspace of ⋂2≤r≤p∗Lr​(σ)\bigcap_{2\leq r\leq p_{*}}L^{r}(\sigma) on which the realizations of the semigroups agree. One may take B⁡(ℋ)B(\mathcal{H}) when all maps are initially defined there. Let 𝒱\mathcal{V} be a linear map with bounded realizations 𝒱(r):Lr​(σ)→Lr​(σ)\mathcal{V}^{(r)}:L^{r}(\sigma)\to L^{r}(\sigma) that agree on 𝒞\mathscr{C}. We assume that adding 𝒱\mathcal{V} to the generator of TtT_{t} generates the semigroup StS_{t}, in the precise sense that, for 0≤t≤t∗0\leq t\leq t_{*}, the following L2L^{2} Trotter formula holds:

St(2)=s−limn→∞⁡(Tt/n(2)​e(t/n)​𝒱(2))n.S_{t}^{(2)}=\operatorname*{s-lim}_{n\to\infty}\bigl(T_{t/n}^{(2)}e^{(t/n)\mathcal{V}^{(2)}}\bigr)^{n}.

Here s−lim\operatorname*{s-lim} denotes convergence on each vector of L2​(σ)L^{2}(\sigma) in its norm. Assume that the perturbation bound

Mt∗:=sup2≤r≤p⁡(t∗)∥𝒱(r):Lr(σ)→Lr(σ)∥M_{t_{*}}:=\sup_{2\leq r\leq p(t_{*})}\|\mathcal{V}^{(r)}:L^{r}(\sigma)\to L^{r}(\sigma)\|

is finite. Then, for 0≤s≤t≤t∗0\leq s\leq t\leq t_{*},

(3.1) ∥St−s:Lp⁡(s)(σ)→Lp⁡(t)(σ)∥≤e(ω+Mt∗)​(t−s).\|S_{t-s}:L^{p(s)}(\sigma)\to L^{p(t)}(\sigma)\|\leq e^{(\omega+M_{t_{*}})(t-s)}.

In particular, ∥St:L2(σ)→Lp⁡(t)(σ)∥≤e(ω+Mt∗)​t\|S_{t}:L^{2}(\sigma)\to L^{p(t)}(\sigma)\|\leq e^{(\omega+M_{t_{*}})t}. If the reverse Trotter formula holds with TT and SS interchanged and perturbation −𝒱-\mathcal{V}, the same statement transfers a curve from SS back to TT.

Proof.

Fix 0≤s<t≤t∗0\leq s<t\leq t_{*} and a positive integer nn. Put h=(t−s)/nh=(t-s)/n and sk=s+k​hs_{k}=s+kh. For X∈𝒞X\in\mathscr{C}, define

X0,n=X,Xk,n=Theh​𝒱Xk−1,n(1≤k≤n).X_{0,n}=X,\qquad X_{k,n}=T_{h}e^{h\mathcal{V}}X_{k-1,n}\quad(1\leq k\leq n).

The products agree wherever two of the weighted spaces overlap, by consistency. The exponential series gives

‖eh​𝒱(p⁡(sk−1))‖≤∑j=0∞hj​Mt∗jj!=eh​Mt∗.\|e^{h\mathcal{V}^{(p(s_{k-1}))}}\|\leq\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac{h^{j}M_{t_{*}}^{j}}{j!}=e^{hM_{t_{*}}}.

‖Xk,n‖p⁡(sk),σ≤eω​h​‖eh​𝒱​Xk−1,n‖p⁡(sk−1),σ≤e(ω+Mt∗)​h​‖Xk−1,n‖p⁡(sk−1),σ.\|X_{k,n}\|_{p(s_{k}),\sigma}\leq e^{\omega h}\|e^{h\mathcal{V}}X_{k-1,n}\|_{p(s_{k-1}),\sigma}\leq e^{(\omega+M_{t_{*}})h}\|X_{k-1,n}\|_{p(s_{k-1}),\sigma}.

Iteration yields a bound independent of nn:

‖Xn,n‖p⁡(t),σ≤e(ω+Mt∗)​(t−s)​‖X‖p⁡(s),σ.\|X_{n,n}\|_{p(t),\sigma}\leq e^{(\omega+M_{t_{*}})(t-s)}\|X\|_{p(s),\sigma}.

We now pass to the limit in Lp⁡(t)​(σ)L^{p(t)}(\sigma). For 2≤q<∞2\leq q<\infty, Hölder’s inequality and Tr⁡σ=1\operatorname{Tr}\sigma=1 give the continuous inclusion Lq​(σ)⊂L2​(σ)L^{q}(\sigma)\subset L^{2}(\sigma):

‖X‖2,σ=‖σ1/4−1/(2​q)​ιq,σ​(X)​σ1/4−1/(2​q)‖2≤‖X‖q,σ.\|X\|_{2,\sigma}=\|\sigma^{1/4-1/(2q)}\iota_{q,\sigma}(X)\sigma^{1/4-1/(2q)}\|_{2}\leq\|X\|_{q,\sigma}.

The bounded sequence (Xn,n)n(X_{n,n})_{n} has a weakly convergent subsequence in the reflexive space Lp⁡(t)​(σ)L^{p(t)}(\sigma), say with limit YY. The same subsequence converges weakly to YY in L2​(σ)L^{2}(\sigma). The Trotter formula also gives

Xn,n=(Th​eh​𝒱)n​X⟶St−s(2)​Xin ​L2​(σ).X_{n,n}=(T_{h}e^{h\mathcal{V}})^{n}X\longrightarrow S_{t-s}^{(2)}X\quad\hbox{in }L^{2}(\sigma).

Uniqueness of the weak limit therefore gives Y=St−s​XY=S_{t-s}X. Weak lower semicontinuity now proves

‖St−s​X‖p⁡(t),σ≤lim infj‖Xnj,nj‖p⁡(t),σ≤e(ω+Mt∗)​(t−s)​‖X‖p⁡(s),σ.\|S_{t-s}X\|_{p(t),\sigma}\leq\liminf_{j}\|X_{n_{j},n_{j}}\|_{p(t),\sigma}\leq e^{(\omega+M_{t_{*}})(t-s)}\|X\|_{p(s),\sigma}.

By density of 𝒞\mathscr{C}, this bound holds on all of Lp⁡(s)​(σ)L^{p(s)}(\sigma). Consistency identifies the limit with St−sS_{t-s}. For s=ts=t the bound is the identity estimate. Replacing 𝒱\mathcal{V} by −𝒱-\mathcal{V} proves the reverse statement whenever the reverse product formula holds. ∎

3.2. Finite-core changes of the Gibbs weight

We now allow the Gibbs weight to change on a finite-dimensional energy subspace and compare the resulting entropies and Dirichlet forms.

Lemma 3.2.

Let σ0\sigma_{0} and σ\sigma be faithful density matrices on ℋ\mathcal{H}. Assume that PP is a finite-rank orthogonal projection satisfying P​σ0=σ0​PP\sigma_{0}=\sigma_{0}P and P​σ=σ​PP\sigma=\sigma P. Set Q=I−PQ=I-P and suppose that

Q​σ​Q=c​Q​σ0​QQ\sigma Q=c\,Q\sigma_{0}Q

for a scalar c>0c>0. Then there is a constant 0≤κ<∞0\leq\kappa<\infty such that, for every Hilbert–Schmidt operator Y∈𝒯2​(ℋ)Y\in\mathscr{T}_{2}(\mathcal{H}) with finite Ent2,σ0⁡(Y)\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma_{0}}(Y),

(3.2) Ent2,σ⁡(Y)≤Ent2,σ0⁡(Y)+κ​‖Y‖22.\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma}(Y)\leq\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma_{0}}(Y)+\kappa\|Y\|_{2}^{2}.
Proof.

The quadratic-form difference K=log⁡σ0−log⁡σK=\log\sigma_{0}-\log\sigma has a bounded self-adjoint extension. Indeed, block functional calculus gives

K=P(logσ0−logσ)P−(logc)Q,∥K∥∞≤max{∥P(logσ0−logσ)P∥∞,|logc|}<∞.K=P(\log\sigma_{0}-\log\sigma)P-(\log c)Q,\qquad\|K\|_{\infty}\leq\max\{\|P(\log\sigma_{0}-\log\sigma)P\|_{\infty},|\log c|\}<\infty.

The PP-block is finite dimensional and both compressed states are strictly positive there. Since the difference of the reference logarithms is bounded, relative entropy satisfies, whenever D(ρ∥σ0)<∞D(\rho\|\sigma_{0})<\infty,

D(ρ∥σ)=D(ρ∥σ0)+Tr(ρK).D(\rho\|\sigma)=D(\rho\|\sigma_{0})+\operatorname{Tr}(\rho K).

This identity holds also when the individual energy and von Neumann entropy traces are infinite, by bounded perturbation of the reference logarithm in the extended relative-entropy definition; see [21, Appendix B.1] for bounded relative Hamiltonians. Apply it to Y†​Y/‖Y‖22Y^{\dagger}Y/\|Y\|_{2}^{2} and Y​Y†/‖Y‖22YY^{\dagger}/\|Y\|_{2}^{2} in the explicit relative-entropy formula for Ent2,σ\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma}. For Y≠0Y\neq 0 this gives

Ent2,σ⁡(Y)−Ent2,σ0⁡(Y)=12​Tr⁡((Y†​Y+Y​Y†)​K)≤‖K‖∞​‖Y‖22.\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma}(Y)-\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma_{0}}(Y)=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{Tr}\bigl((Y^{\dagger}Y+YY^{\dagger})K\bigr)\leq\|K\|_{\infty}\|Y\|_{2}^{2}.

For Y=0Y=0 the claim is immediate. Thus one may take κ=‖log⁡σ0−log⁡σ‖∞\kappa=\|\log\sigma_{0}-\log\sigma\|_{\infty}. ∎

Proposition 3.3.

Let Tt0T_{t}^{0} and TtT_{t} be primitive KMS-symmetric Markov semigroups with faithful invariant states σ0\sigma_{0} and σ\sigma, and let L0,L≥0L_{0},L\geq 0 be their standard-form generators with closed forms ℰ0,ℰ\mathcal{E}_{0},\mathcal{E} on 𝒯2​(ℋ)\mathscr{T}_{2}(\mathcal{H}). Assume the finite-core relation of Lemma 3.2, and choose its comparison constant κ≥0\kappa\geq 0. Suppose that, for some finite c0>0c_{0}>0,

Ent2,σ0⁡(Y)≤c0​ℰ0​(Y),Y∈D⁡(ℰ0).\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma_{0}}(Y)\leq c_{0}\mathcal{E}_{0}(Y),\qquad Y\in D(\mathcal{E}_{0}).

Assume also that D⁡(ℰ)⊂D⁡(ℰ0)D(\mathcal{E})\subset D(\mathcal{E}_{0}) and that there are finite constants A>0A>0 and B≥0B\geq 0 such that

(3.3) ℰ0​(Y)≤A​ℰ​(Y)+B​‖Y‖22,Y∈D⁡(ℰ).\mathcal{E}_{0}(Y)\leq A\mathcal{E}(Y)+B\|Y\|_{2}^{2},\qquad Y\in D(\mathcal{E}).

If LL has gap λ>0\lambda>0, define cfc=c0​A+(c0​B+κ+2)/λc_{\rm fc}=c_{0}A+(c_{0}B+\kappa+2)/\lambda. Then

(3.4) Ent2,σ⁡(Y)≤cfc​ℰ​(Y),Y∈D⁡(ℰ).\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma}(Y)\leq c_{\rm fc}\mathcal{E}(Y),\qquad Y\in D(\mathcal{E}).

This conclusion concerns the 22-logarithmic Sobolev inequality. We do not deduce a hypercontractive bound from these assumptions.

Proof.

Fix X∈D⁡(ℰ)X\in D(\mathcal{E}) and define its centred vector by Y=X−⟨σ,X⟩​σY=X-\langle\sqrt{\sigma},X\rangle\sqrt{\sigma}. Since σ∈ker⁡L\sqrt{\sigma}\in\ker L, both XX and YY belong to D⁡(ℰ)⊂D⁡(ℰ0)D(\mathcal{E})\subset D(\mathcal{E}_{0}). The free logarithmic Sobolev inequality and Lemma 3.2 first give

Ent2,σ⁡(Y)≤Ent2,σ0⁡(Y)+κ​‖Y‖22≤c0​ℰ0​(Y)+κ​‖Y‖22<∞.\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma}(Y)\leq\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma_{0}}(Y)+\kappa\|Y\|_{2}^{2}\leq c_{0}\mathcal{E}_{0}(Y)+\kappa\|Y\|_{2}^{2}<\infty.

Thus Lemma 2.4 applies to YY without an endpoint assumption. Combining it with (3.3) gives

Ent2,σ⁡(X)≤Ent2,σ⁡(Y)+2​‖Y‖22≤c0​A​ℰ​(X)+(c0​B+κ+2)​‖Y‖22.\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma}(X)\leq\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma}(Y)+2\|Y\|_{2}^{2}\leq c_{0}A\mathcal{E}(X)+(c_{0}B+\kappa+2)\|Y\|_{2}^{2}.

The centering does not change the energy, and the gap controls its norm:

L1/2​Y=L1/2​X,λ​‖Y‖22≤‖L1/2​Y‖22=ℰ⁡(X).L^{1/2}Y=L^{1/2}X,\qquad\lambda\|Y\|_{2}^{2}\leq\|L^{1/2}Y\|_{2}^{2}=\mathcal{E}(X).

Substitution removes the squared-norm term:

Ent2,σ⁡(X)≤(c0​A+c0​B+κ+2λ)​ℰ​(X)=cfc​ℰ​(X).\operatorname{Ent}_{2,\sigma}(X)\leq\left(c_{0}A+\frac{c_{0}B+\kappa+2}{\lambda}\right)\mathcal{E}(X)=c_{\rm fc}\mathcal{E}(X).

To deduce hypercontractivity from a logarithmic Sobolev inequality, one needs regularity of the LpL^{p} Dirichlet forms [8, 9]. We prove an L2L^{2}-to-L4L^{4} bound directly for the Coulomb sampler in Section 4.2. ∎

4. Applications and obstructions

We apply the entropy-decay criteria to bosonic Gibbs samplers and examine how the jump operators affect hypercontractivity. We classify one-mode polynomial jumps by their order and then treat Bose–Hubbard models with hopping. For finite-rank Coulomb perturbations, we use a weighted oscillator estimate. A periodic charging model then shows that a positive spectral gap can coexist with failure of every L2L^{2}-to-LpL^{p} endpoint with p>2p>2.

4.1. Polynomial jumps and multimode Bose–Hubbard models

We first compare the growth of a one-mode number Hamiltonian with the order of the bosonic jumps. This gives a classification of the hypercontractive endpoints and explains why cubic jumps suffice for quadratic number Hamiltonians. We then prove exponential entropy decay for a full multimode Bose–Hubbard sampler with hopping and repulsive density interactions in Theorem 4.3.

Entropy decay for quantum Ornstein–Uhlenbeck semigroups, with Hamiltonians quadratic in the creation and annihilation operators, is well understood; see, for example, [28, 29, 30]. Here the Hamiltonian is a nonlinear polynomial of the number operator, and the filtered transition rates depend strongly on occupation number.

We use the bosonic operators of Section 2.1 on the one-mode space ℋ=ℓ2​(ℕ0)\mathcal{H}=\ell^{2}(\mathbb{N}_{0}), omitting their mode index. Let H=h⁡(N)H=h(N), where hh is a real polynomial of degree m≥2m\geq 2 with positive leading coefficient, and fix β>0\beta>0. The occupation number is denoted by nn, and Zβ=∑n≥0e−β​h​(n)Z_{\beta}=\sum_{n\geq 0}e^{-\beta h(n)}. A jump of order d≥1d\geq 1 creates or annihilates dd particles; we use the adjoint pair 𝒜d={ad,(a†)d}\mathcal{A}_{d}=\{a^{d},(a^{\dagger})^{d}\}. Choose a finite nonempty set D⊂{1,2,…}D\subset\{1,2,\ldots\} of jump orders, put d∗:=max⁡Dd_{*}:=\max D, and take the bare family 𝒜D:=⋃d∈D𝒜d\mathcal{A}_{D}:=\bigcup_{d\in D}\mathcal{A}_{d}. The set DD is unrelated to the relative entropy D(ρ∥σ)D(\rho\|\sigma).

Theorem 4.2 gives three regimes: no hypercontractive endpoint when d∗<md_{*}<m, a positive waiting time when d∗=md_{*}=m, and an endpoint at every positive time when d∗>md_{*}>m. When d∗=md_{*}=m, the theorem gives the threshold but excludes the boundary time from its statement. The proof compares the growth of the Gibbs weight, governed by h⁡(n)h(n), with the diagonal damping of order nd∗n^{d_{*}}. The remaining terms are uniformly bounded over compact intervals of finite exponents and can be treated by Theorem 3.1. A no-jump lower bound in the invariant diagonal sector gives the converse estimates.

Separating the diagonal loss.

We first work with one jump pair and identify the unbounded part of its generator. We first prove the matrix formulas on the finite-rank core span{En​k:n,k≥0}\operatorname{span}\{E_{nk}:n,k\geq 0\}, where En​k=|n⟩​⟨k|E_{nk}=|n\rangle\langle k|. For the filter (2.3), the dressed creation and annihilation jumps are denoted by Ld+L_{d}^{+} and Ld−L_{d}^{-}, respectively:

Ld+=(a†)d​f^ℳ​(h⁡(N+d)−h⁡(N)),Ld−=ad​f^ℳ​(h⁡(N−d)−h⁡(N)).L_{d}^{+}=(a^{\dagger})^{d}\widehat{f}_{\!\mathscr{M}}(h(N+d)-h(N)),\qquad L_{d}^{-}=a^{d}\widehat{f}_{\!\mathscr{M}}(h(N-d)-h(N)).

Put

Δd+​h​(n)=h⁡(n+d)−h⁡(n),Δd−​h​(n)=h⁡(n−d)−h⁡(n),\Delta_{d}^{+}h(n)=h(n+d)-h(n),\qquad\Delta_{d}^{-}h(n)=h(n-d)-h(n),

Here h⁡(n−d)h(n-d) means evaluation of the polynomial at the integer n−dn-d. For n<dn<d, the lowering jump is zero, so no transition to a negative occupation occurs. Every falling factorial below is defined to be zero when n<dn<d. To use the perturbation theorem, we need bounds on the weighted generator. Conjugation changes the gain operators and leaves the diagonal losses unchanged. On the symmetric Schatten realization of Lp​(σβ)L^{p}(\sigma_{\beta}), for 2≤p<∞2\leq p<\infty define

gd,±,p​(n)=f^ℳ​(Δd±​h​(n))​eβ⁡(p−1)​Δd±​h​(n)/(2​p)=exp⁡[−1+(β​Δd±​h​(n))24+(p−2)​β​Δd±​h​(n)4​p]g_{d,\pm,p}(n)=\widehat{f}_{\!\mathscr{M}}(\Delta_{d}^{\pm}h(n))e^{\beta(p-1)\Delta_{d}^{\pm}h(n)/(2p)}=\exp\left[-\frac{\sqrt{1+(\beta\Delta_{d}^{\pm}h(n))^{2}}}{4}+\frac{(p-2)\beta\Delta_{d}^{\pm}h(n)}{4p}\right]

and

Bd,+,p\displaystyle B_{d,+,p} =(a†)d​gd,+,p​(N),\displaystyle=(a^{\dagger})^{d}g_{d,+,p}(N), Bd,−,p\displaystyle B_{d,-,p} =ad​gd,−,p​(N),\displaystyle=a^{d}g_{d,-,p}(N),
bd,+​(N)\displaystyle b_{d,+}(N) =∏j=1d(N+j)​|f^ℳ​(Δd+​h​(N))|2,\displaystyle=\prod_{j=1}^{d}(N+j)|\widehat{f}_{\!\mathscr{M}}(\Delta_{d}^{+}h(N))|^{2}, bd,−​(N)\displaystyle b_{d,-}(N) =∏j=0d−1(N−j)​|f^ℳ​(Δd−​h​(N))|2.\displaystyle=\prod_{j=0}^{d-1}(N-j)|\widehat{f}_{\!\mathscr{M}}(\Delta_{d}^{-}h(N))|^{2}.

The symbols Bd,±,pB_{d,\pm,p} denote the transported Heisenberg gain operators, and bd,±​(N)b_{d,\pm}(N) denote the diagonal loss operators. Indeed, transport of the gain L†​X​LL^{\dagger}XL gives σβ1/(2​p)L†σβ−1/(2p)\sigma_{\beta}^{1/(2p)}L^{\dagger}\sigma_{\beta}^{-1/(2p)}. Relabelling the adjoint pair and using the KMS relation gives the factor (p−1)/(2​p)(p-1)/(2p) above. In particular the transported generator annihilates σβ1/p\sigma_{\beta}^{1/p}, the vector representing II. The weighted generator of the ddth jump pair, acting on its symmetric Schatten realization, is

ℒp,h,d​(X)=Bd,+,p​X​Bd,+,p†+Bd,−,p​X​Bd,−,p†−12​{bd,+​(N)+bd,−​(N),X}.\mathscr{L}_{p,h,d}(X)=B_{d,+,p}XB_{d,+,p}^{\dagger}+B_{d,-,p}XB_{d,-,p}^{\dagger}-\frac{1}{2}\{b_{d,+}(N)+b_{d,-}(N),X\}.

The full multimode Bose–Hubbard Hamiltonian.

With hopping, the filtered jumps are no longer explicit in the occupation basis. Total particle number is still conserved, so we can estimate the filters on finite-dimensional particle sectors. The cubic losses dominate the errors in these estimates.

12​dd​t​‖UM​(t)‖22≤(θ∗/s−c)​⟨UM,H~​UM+UM​H~⟩+Cc,θ∗​‖UM​(t)‖22.\frac{1}{2}\frac{\,\mathrm{d}}{\,\mathrm{d}t}\|U_{M}(t)\|_{2}^{2}\leq(\theta_{*}/s-c)\langle U_{M},\widetilde{H}U_{M}+U_{M}\widetilde{H}\rangle+C_{c,\theta_{*}}\|U_{M}(t)\|_{2}^{2}.

Integration and the same form-core limit and Fatou argument give ∥Ts:L2(σβ)→Lp(σβ)∥≤Z~1/2−1/pes​Cc,θ∗<∞\|T_{s}:L^{2}(\sigma_{\beta})\to L^{p}(\sigma_{\beta})\|\leq\widetilde{Z}^{1/2-1/p}e^{sC_{c,\theta_{*}}}<\infty. The quadratic form domain embeds compactly into Hilbert–Schmidt space. Step 7’s kernel argument uses only the linear rows and applies unchanged, giving a simple kernel and a positive gap. Remark 4.4.

For k=1k=1, U1=2U_{1}=2, and μ1=−1\mu_{1}=-1, the Hamiltonian is N2N^{2}. The linear pair alone has no bounded L2L^{2}-to-L4L^{4} endpoint by Theorem 4.2; the quadratic pair gives a finite waiting time, and the cubic pair gives smoothing at every positive time. The theorem treats both enlarged families with full hopping. It does not give the same entropy estimate for the samplers with only linear jumps in [14], nor a rate uniform in the number of modes.

4.2. Finite-rank Coulomb truncations

We next treat a trapped Coulomb system in two or three dimensions. The interaction is compressed to a finite Hermite subspace, while the Hamiltonian and sampler act on the full infinite-dimensional space. For each fixed particle number and cutoff, we prove a bounded L2L^{2}-to-L4L^{4} map and exponential entropy decay.

Thus the closed form on D⁡(𝒦1/2)D(\mathcal{K}^{1/2}) also annihilates σ\sqrt{\sigma}. For 𝖯J=𝟏[0,J]​(𝒦)\mathsf{P}_{J}=\mathbf{1}_{[0,J]}(\mathcal{K}), this gives

so adding σ\sqrt{\sigma} does not change the closed form. This proves that ℱ\mathscr{F} is a form core for the constructed operator LL; the coefficient formula also gives ℱ⊂D⁡(L)\mathscr{F}\subset D(L). The parameters in Lemma 4.6 can now be chosen as

because c/v=cosh⁡βc/v=\cosh\beta. The lemma gives (4.10).

Step 3: the endpoint and entropy decay. The operator B∗=σ−1/8e−β𝖭/4B_{*}=\sigma^{-1/8}e^{-\beta\mathsf{N}/4} has a bounded extension. Since H0,n=k+2​𝖭H_{0,n}=k+2\mathsf{N}, its two blocks are

≤‖B∗‖∞2​‖e(β/4)​𝒦​Y‖4≤‖B∗‖∞2​‖e(β/4)​𝒦​Y‖2.\displaystyle\leq\|B_{*}\|_{\infty}^{2}\|e^{(\beta/4)\mathcal{K}}Y\|_{4}\leq\|B_{*}\|_{\infty}^{2}\|e^{(\beta/4)\mathcal{K}}Y\|_{2}.

‖(I−𝖯J)​X‖22≤‖(𝒦+I)1/2​X‖22J+1≤ℰ⁡(X)+c2​‖X‖22c1​(J+1).\|(I-\mathsf{P}_{J})X\|_{2}^{2}\leq\frac{\|(\mathcal{K}+I)^{1/2}X\|_{2}^{2}}{J+1}\leq\frac{\mathcal{E}(X)+c_{2}\|X\|_{2}^{2}}{c_{1}(J+1)}.

4.3. A bounded-rate obstruction

We show that bounded escape rates can prevent hypercontractivity even when the Gibbs state is strongly confining and the sampler has a positive spectral gap.

Proposition 4.7.

Let TtT_{t} be a conservative continuous-time Markov semigroup on a countable set Ω\Omega with faithful invariant probability π\pi. For distinct x,y∈Ωx,y\in\Omega, let q⁡(x,y)≥0q(x,y)\geq 0 be the transition rate from xx to yy, and put q⁡(x)=∑y≠xq⁡(x,y)q(x)=\sum_{y\neq x}q(x,y), the total rate out of xx. Here Lp​(π)L^{p}(\pi) has norm ‖f‖p,π=(∑x∈Ωπ⁡(x)​|f⁡(x)|p)1/p\|f\|_{p,\pi}=(\sum_{x\in\Omega}\pi(x)|f(x)|^{p})^{1/p}. If there are points xkx_{k} such that

π⁡(xk)⟶0,supkq⁡(xk)≤Λ<∞,\pi(x_{k})\longrightarrow 0,\qquad\sup_{k}q(x_{k})\leq\Lambda<\infty,

then for every p>2p>2 and every finite t>0t>0,

∥Tt:L2(π)→Lp(π)∥=∞.\|T_{t}:L^{2}(\pi)\to L^{p}(\pi)\|=\infty.
Proof.

Let 𝟏{xk}\mathbf{1}_{\{x_{k}\}} be the indicator of the singleton {xk}\{x_{k}\} and set fk=π(xk)−1/2𝟏{xk}f_{k}=\pi(x_{k})^{-1/2}\mathbf{1}_{\{x_{k}\}}, so ‖fk‖2,π=1\|f_{k}\|_{2,\pi}=1. The event that the chain makes no jump before time tt has probability at least e−Λ​te^{-\Lambda t} when it starts from xkx_{k}. Hence

(Ttfk)(xk)≥e−Λ​tπ(xk)−1/2(T_{t}f_{k})(x_{k})\geq e^{-\Lambda t}\pi(x_{k})^{-1/2}

and therefore ‖Tt​fk‖p,π≥e−Λ​t​π​(xk)1/p−1/2⟶∞.\|T_{t}f_{k}\|_{p,\pi}\geq e^{-\Lambda t}\pi(x_{k})^{1/p-1/2}\longrightarrow\infty. ∎

Consider now the one-mode periodic charging model on ℓ2​(ℤ)\ell^{2}(\mathbb{Z}), with charge basis (em)m∈ℤ(e_{m})_{m\in\mathbb{Z}}. Define the charge operator 𝗇​em=m​em\mathsf{n}e_{m}=me_{m} and the bilateral shift S​em=em+1Se_{m}=e_{m+1}. Let H=h⁡(𝗇)H=h(\mathsf{n}), where hh is a nonconstant even polynomial (h⁡(−m)=h⁡(m)h(-m)=h(m)) with positive leading coefficient, and use bare jumps S,S†,𝗇S,S^{\dagger},\mathsf{n}. The charge operator 𝗇\mathsf{n} is distinct from the particle count nn of the preceding application. The charge row alone generates the conservative dephasing semigroup

(Φtcharge(ρ))m​k=e−t|f^ℳ(0)|2(m−k)2/2ρm​k.(\Phi_{t}^{\rm charge}(\rho))_{mk}=e^{-t|\widehat{f}_{\!\mathscr{M}}(0)|^{2}(m-k)^{2}/2}\rho_{mk}.

The two filtered shifts are bounded, and their loss operators are diagonal, so the correction Hamiltonian is zero. Their bounded GKLS generator perturbs this dephasing generator. The bounded perturbation product formula gives a conservative completely positive semigroup; the KMS pairing of the shifts makes the Gibbs state invariant. For a diagonal observable g⁡(𝗇)g(\mathsf{n}), with g:ℤ→ℂg:\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{C}, the charge row vanishes. The invariant diagonal sector is the birth–death chain with generator QQ given by

(Q​g)​(m)=rm+​(g⁡(m+1)−g⁡(m))+rm−​(g⁡(m−1)−g⁡(m)),rm±=|f^ℳ​(h⁡(m±1)−h⁡(m))|2.(Qg)(m)=r_{m}^{+}\bigl(g(m+1)-g(m)\bigr)+r_{m}^{-}\bigl(g(m-1)-g(m)\bigr),\qquad r_{m}^{\pm}=|\widehat{f}_{\!\mathscr{M}}(h(m\pm 1)-h(m))|^{2}.

The filter (2.3) gives 0≤rm±≤10\leq r_{m}^{\pm}\leq 1. Its invariant probability is

Zch=∑m∈ℤe−β​h​(m),πm=Zch−1​e−β​h​(m),σch=∑m∈ℤπm​|em⟩​⟨em|.Z_{\rm ch}=\sum_{m\in\mathbb{Z}}e^{-\beta h(m)},\qquad\pi_{m}=Z_{\rm ch}^{-1}e^{-\beta h(m)},\qquad\sigma_{\rm ch}=\sum_{m\in\mathbb{Z}}\pi_{m}|e_{m}\rangle\langle e_{m}|.

Since diagonal observables satisfy ‖g⁡(𝗇)‖p,σch=‖g‖p,π\|g(\mathsf{n})\|_{p,\sigma_{\rm ch}}=\|g\|_{p,\pi}, the classical norm bound is a lower bound for the quantum norm. One has πm→0\pi_{m}\to 0 as |m|→∞|m|\to\infty, while the holding rates satisfy rm++rm−≤2r_{m}^{+}+r_{m}^{-}\leq 2. Thus Proposition 4.7 shows that this invariant diagonal sector, and hence the full quantum semigroup, has no finite-time L2L^{2}-to-LpL^{p} endpoint for any p>2p>2. This gives a periodic-charge counterpart of the m>d∗m>d_{*} obstruction above. The sampler nevertheless has a positive gap. We prove this separately on the diagonal and off-diagonal sectors. After the unitary map g↦(πm​g​(m))mg\mapsto(\sqrt{\pi_{m}}g(m))_{m}, the negative diagonal generator is the Jacobi operator with diagonal rm++rm−r_{m}^{+}+r_{m}^{-} and off-diagonal entries −rm+​rm+1−-\sqrt{r_{m}^{+}r_{m+1}^{-}}. Since hh is an even confining polynomial,

rm++rm−⟶1,rm+​rm+1−⟶0(|m|→∞).r_{m}^{+}+r_{m}^{-}\longrightarrow 1,\qquad\sqrt{r_{m}^{+}r_{m+1}^{-}}\longrightarrow 0\qquad(|m|\to\infty).

Thus the transformed operator is I+KI+K, where KK is compact: its three diagonals vanish at infinity and are norm limits of their finite truncations. In particular its essential spectrum is {1}\{1\}. The reversible classical form is

⟨g,−Q​g⟩L2​(π)=∑m∈ℤπm​rm+​|g⁡(m+1)−g⁡(m)|2.\langle g,-Qg\rangle_{L^{2}(\pi)}=\sum_{m\in\mathbb{Z}}\pi_{m}r_{m}^{+}|g(m+1)-g(m)|^{2}.

Every coefficient is positive. Thus zero energy forces g⁡(m+1)=g⁡(m)g(m+1)=g(m) for every mm, so gg is constant. After the unitary change of variables the kernel is ℂ​(πm)m\mathbb{C}(\sqrt{\pi_{m}})_{m}. Since zero lies outside the essential spectrum {1}\{1\}, it is an isolated simple eigenvalue, and

λdiag=inf(spec⁡(−Q)∖{0})>0.\lambda_{\rm diag}=\inf(\operatorname{spec}(-Q)\setminus\{0\})>0.

The diagonal and off-diagonal Hilbert–Schmidt subspaces reduce the standard-form generator: each shift gain moves the two charge indices by the same amount, and the loss operators are diagonal. The charge row contributes the nonnegative form

ℰcharge​(Y)=|f^ℳ​(0)|22​∑m,k∈ℤ(m−k)2​|Ym​k|2≥e−1/22​‖Yoff‖22.\mathcal{E}_{\rm charge}(Y)=\frac{|\widehat{f}_{\!\mathscr{M}}(0)|^{2}}{2}\sum_{m,k\in\mathbb{Z}}(m-k)^{2}|Y_{mk}|^{2}\geq\frac{e^{-1/2}}{2}\|Y_{\rm off}\|_{2}^{2}.

The other rows have a nonnegative total form. Consequently the full sampler is primitive and has gap at least min{λdiag,e−1/2/2}>0\min\{\lambda_{\rm diag},e^{-1/2}/2\}>0. Thus this model has a positive gap but no bounded L2L^{2}-to-LpL^{p} map at any finite time, for any p>2p>2.
